detailedAnswer: Checked exceptions must be declared or handled, and they are meant for recoverable conditions such as a missing file or a failed network call, while unchecked exceptions usually signal programming errors such as a null dereference or an illegal argument. Overusing checked exceptions leaks implementation details through every caller, so many modern codebases wrap them in a meaningful unchecked exception at a boundary. Try-with-resources guarantees that each resource is closed in reverse order of opening, even when an exception occurs, and any exception thrown during close is added as a suppressed exception rather than hiding the original failure. Always close resources you open, log the original exception with context, and avoid catching Exception just to swallow it.
followUps: When would you wrap a checked exception instead of declaring it?
How do you inspect a suppressed exception?
question: When should you use a checked exception versus an unchecked exception, and how does try-with-resources change exception handling?
shortAnswer: Checked for recoverable conditions, unchecked for programming errors; try-with-resources closes resources reliably and preserves the original exception, adding close failures as suppressed exceptions.
tips: Name a concrete recoverable case and a concrete programming-error case.
Mention suppressed exceptions — it shows you have debugged real resource code.
title: Checked vs unchecked exceptions

detailedAnswer: HashMap is not thread-safe and its iterators are fail-fast, so a concurrent modification during iteration usually throws ConcurrentModificationException, whereas ConcurrentHashMap iterators are weakly consistent and tolerate concurrent updates without throwing. ConcurrentHashMap also forbids null keys and null values, because a null return from get would be ambiguous when another thread could have removed the entry. Its atomic methods such as computeIfAbsent, merge, and putIfAbsent let you update a shared map without external locking, but the mapping function must be short and side-effect free, since it may be retried. For counters or grouped results, combine it with atomic values such as LongAdder or a concurrent collection rather than synchronizing the whole map.
followUps: Why does ConcurrentHashMap forbid null keys and values?
When is computeIfAbsent unsafe?
question: How does ConcurrentHashMap differ from a synchronized HashMap, and when would you choose it?
shortAnswer: ConcurrentHashMap is lock-striped, thread-safe, weakly consistent for iteration, and forbids nulls; a synchronized HashMap serializes all access and still fails fast on concurrent iteration.
tips: Contrast fail-fast with weakly consistent iteration explicitly.
Warn that computeIfAbsent functions must be short and side-effect free.
title: ConcurrentHashMap vs synchronized HashMap

detailedAnswer: Parallel streams split work across the common ForkJoinPool, which helps only for large, CPU-bound, splittable workloads with independent, non-blocking operations. They hurt when the source is small, the work is I/O-bound, the operations block, or the pipeline uses stateful operations such as sorted or distinct that force coordination, and they can starve other tasks sharing the common pool. Stateful lambda side effects, such as appending to a shared list, break correctness in parallel pipelines, so collect results with a proper collector instead. A good answer names the workload, checks its size, avoids blocking calls, and measures before and after rather than assuming parallelism is faster.
followUps: Why should you not do blocking I/O inside a parallel stream?
How do you collect results safely from a parallel stream?
question: When does a parallel stream help, and when does it make performance worse?
shortAnswer: Parallel streams help only for large CPU-bound work over a splittable source; they hurt for small, blocking, or I/O-bound work and can starve the shared common pool.
tips: Give the three conditions: large, CPU-bound, splittable.
Mention that the common ForkJoinPool is shared, so a slow stream affects the whole application.
title: Parallel streams: help or harm

detailedAnswer: CompletableFuture chains such as thenApply, thenCompose, and thenCombine let you express dependent and independent async steps without blocking, while exceptionally and handle let you recover or translate failures at a defined point in the chain. The most common production failure is submitting many futures to an unbounded or too-small pool, so dependent stages queue up and the whole pipeline stalls even though no thread has deadlocked. Always supply an explicit executor for blocking or long-running stages, bound the pool and its queue, set timeouts with orTimeout, and decide where exceptions are observed, because an unobserved future failure is silently lost. For fan-out work, combine futures with allOf and then inspect each result individually rather than assuming success.
followUps: What happens when a CompletableFuture exception is never observed?
Why should blocking stages not use the common ForkJoinPool?
question: How do you chain CompletableFuture stages safely in production, and what usually goes wrong?
shortAnswer: Chain with thenApply, thenCompose, and thenCombine, handle failures explicitly, use a dedicated bounded executor for blocking stages, and apply timeouts.
tips: Name the thread-pool exhaustion failure mode, not just the API methods.
Mention orTimeout and explicit exception handling in the same answer.
title: CompletableFuture in production

detailedAnswer: Most modern collectors divide the heap into young and old generations, because most objects die young: short-lived objects are collected cheaply in the young generation, while survivors are promoted to the old generation, which is collected less often but more expensively. G1 divides the heap into regions and targets a pause-time goal by collecting the regions with the most garbage first, whereas the Parallel collector prioritizes throughput and accepts longer pauses. Frequent full garbage collections, long promotion failures, or a steadily growing old generation usually point to a leak, an undersized heap, or objects that live longer than expected. Tune by measuring pause times and allocation rates first, then adjust heap size and collector choice, rather than guessing flags.
followUps: How do you tell a leak apart from a heap that is simply too small?
When would you prefer throughput over low pause time?
question: How do generational garbage collectors work, and how do you choose between G1 and Parallel GC?
shortAnswer: Young objects are collected cheaply and survivors are promoted; G1 targets pause time with region-based collection, Parallel targets throughput with longer pauses.
tips: Explain the generational hypothesis before naming collectors.
Tie the choice to a measurable goal: pause time versus throughput.
title: Generational GC and collector choice

detailedAnswer: Singleton is the default scope, so the container creates one instance per application context, while prototype creates a new instance on every request for the bean. The classic trap is injecting a prototype bean into a singleton: the injection happens once, so the singleton keeps the same prototype instance forever. Fix it by injecting a provider, such as ObjectProvider or Provider, and asking for a fresh instance on each use, or by using a scoped proxy. Request and session scopes only exist in a web context, and relying on them in a service layer makes the service untestable outside a request, so keep scope decisions at the edge where they belong.
followUps: How do you get a fresh prototype instance inside a singleton?
Why is request scope a poor fit for a service bean?
question: What goes wrong when a prototype bean is injected into a singleton, and how do you fix it?
shortAnswer: The singleton captures one prototype instance at injection time; inject ObjectProvider or Provider and request a fresh instance per use, or use a scoped proxy.
tips: State the trap first, then the fix — interviewers want both.
Mention that prototype beans are not destroyed by the container.
title: Prototype beans in singletons

detailedAnswer: Spring Boot resolves configuration from many sources in a defined precedence order, roughly: command-line arguments and environment variables beat application properties files, which beat packaged defaults, and profile-specific files such as application-prod.properties beat the base application.properties within the same source type. Binding properties into a validated @ConfigurationProperties class is safer than scattering @Value annotations, because it groups related settings, supports relaxed binding and type conversion, and fails fast on invalid values when validation is enabled. Secrets should come from environment variables or a secret store, never from a committed properties file, and profile-specific behaviour should be expressed as configuration, not as if-statements scattered through code. When a value surprises you, check the active profiles and the effective property source order before assuming the code is wrong.
followUps: Where should secrets live, and why not in application.properties?
How do you fail fast on invalid configuration?
question: How does Spring Boot decide which configuration value wins, and how should you structure configuration for multiple environments?
shortAnswer: Higher-precedence sources such as command-line arguments and environment variables beat properties files, and profile-specific files beat the base file; bind settings into validated @ConfigurationProperties classes.
tips: Recite the precedence order in one sentence.
Recommend @ConfigurationProperties over scattered @Value.
title: Profiles and configuration precedence

detailedAnswer: A @RestControllerAdvice class centralizes exception handling across controllers, mapping each exception type to a consistent error body and HTTP status, so controllers stay focused on happy-path logic. Bean Validation annotations such as @NotNull, @Size, and @Pattern on a request DTO, triggered by @Valid, reject bad input before business logic runs, and validation failures arrive as a MethodArgumentNotValidException you can translate in the same advice class. Return ResponseEntity when the status or headers vary, such as 201 Created with a Location header after creating a resource, and keep error bodies stable with fields for a code, a message, and request context. Never leak stack traces or internal exception messages to clients, and never use exceptions for ordinary control flow.
followUps: Where does validation run relative to controller logic?
What should a stable API error body contain?
question: How do you design consistent error handling and validation for a Spring MVC REST API?
shortAnswer: Validate DTOs with Bean Validation, translate exceptions centrally in @RestControllerAdvice into stable error bodies, and use ResponseEntity when status or headers vary.
tips: Pair validation and exception translation — they belong together in the answer.
Mention 201 with a Location header as the ResponseEntity example.
title: REST error handling and validation

detailedAnswer: Derived query methods are readable for simple lookups, but they grow unwieldy for complex conditions, so use @Query for explicit JPQL or native SQL, and projections or DTO queries when you only need a few columns. Pagination with Pageable is convenient, but offset pagination degrades on large tables because the database still scans skipped rows, so keyset pagination on an ordered unique key is better for infinite-scroll or export workloads. Keep transaction boundaries at the service layer, not the repository, so a unit of work that touches several repositories commits or rolls back together, and avoid lazy-loading collections inside a controller after the transaction has closed. Count queries for Page results can also be expensive, so use Slice or a separate count only when the total is actually displayed.
followUps: When is keyset pagination better than offset pagination?
Why should transactions live at the service layer?
question: How do you choose between derived queries, @Query, and pagination strategies in Spring Data JPA?
shortAnswer: Derived queries for simple lookups, @Query for complex or selective queries, offset pagination for small result sets, and keyset pagination for large or scrolling workloads.
tips: Name the offset-pagination cost: skipped rows are still scanned.
Put transactions at the service layer, not the repository.
title: JPA queries and pagination

detailedAnswer: A microservice deployment typically needs service discovery so instances can find each other as they scale, centralized configuration so behaviour changes without redeploying, and a resilience layer with timeouts, retries with backoff, and circuit breakers. Timeouts bound how long you wait, retries help only for transient and idempotent failures, and a circuit breaker stops calling a failing dependency so it can recover instead of being overwhelmed by retries. Retrying a non-idempotent operation, such as a payment, without an idempotency key can duplicate its effect, so retry policy and idempotency must be designed together. Health endpoints and distributed tracing are what let you find the failing service in the first place, so treat observability as part of the design, not an afterthought.
followUps: When is a retry dangerous rather than helpful?
How do a timeout, a retry, and a circuit breaker complement each other?
question: What resilience patterns does a microservice need, and when does each one apply?
shortAnswer: Service discovery, centralized configuration, timeouts to bound waits, retries only for transient idempotent failures, and circuit breakers to stop overwhelming a failing dependency.
tips: Distinguish retries from circuit breakers by their purpose.
Flag non-idempotent retries, such as payments, as the classic mistake.
title: Microservice resilience patterns

detailedAnswer: An inner join returns only rows with a match on both sides, a left join keeps every row from the left table and fills unmatched right-side columns with null, and a full outer join keeps unmatched rows from both sides. To find duplicates, group by the candidate columns and keep only groups whose count is greater than one; to find orphan rows, use a left join and filter for null on the right side, or an anti-join with NOT EXISTS. Indexes speed up filtered and joined columns, but every index slows writes and costs storage, so index the columns your queries actually filter and join on, and verify with an execution plan rather than guessing. A common mistake is joining on a column with a different type or collation, which silently prevents index use.
followUps: How would you find customers with no orders?
Why can adding an index make some queries slower?
question: How do join types differ, and how would you find duplicate and orphan rows in SQL?
shortAnswer: Inner keeps only matches, left keeps all left rows with nulls for misses, full outer keeps both sides; find duplicates with GROUP BY and HAVING COUNT greater than one, orphans with a left join filtered to null.
tips: Give the orphan-row query pattern, not just the join definitions.
Mention checking the execution plan before adding indexes.
title: SQL joins, duplicates, and orphans

detailedAnswer: The task is to group words that are anagrams of each other, for example listen and silent. The idiomatic approach is a single pass over the input: for each word, build a canonical key by sorting its characters or by counting character frequencies, then append the word to the list stored under that key in a hash map. Sorting gives a key in time proportional to word length times log word length, while a frequency count gives a linear-time key and is preferable for long words. At the end, return the map values as the groups. A common mistake is comparing words pairwise, which is quadratic, or using the unsorted word itself as the key, which never groups anything.
followUps: How would you improve the key for very long words?
How does the complexity change if the alphabet is tiny, such as lowercase letters only?
question: Coding task: group a list of words into sets of anagrams. What is your approach and its complexity?
shortAnswer: Build a canonical key per word, by sorted characters or character counts, and collect words into a hash map keyed by that key; each word is processed once.
tips: State the key idea first — the rest of the solution follows from it.
Compare sorting versus counting keys to show you considered trade-offs.
title: Coding: group anagrams

detailedAnswer: Start by reproducing the slowness with a realistic request and measuring where time goes: check application metrics for thread-pool saturation, database connection-pool waits, and cache hit rates, and enable slow-query logging before changing anything. The usual culprits, in order, are an N+1 query pattern introduced by a new feature, a missing index on a newly filtered column, an unbounded result set being serialized, and a downstream call without a timeout. Fix the query or add the index, page or limit the result, add a timeout and a cache only where the data tolerates staleness, and verify with the same measurement you started from. A common mistake is adding caching or scaling instances first, which hides the bad query and spreads its cost across more machines.
followUps: How do you confirm an N+1 problem rather than guessing?
When is adding a cache the wrong fix?
question: Scenario: a REST endpoint that used to respond in 200ms now takes 5 seconds under load, with no recent deployment. How do you investigate and fix it?
shortAnswer: Measure first — thread pool, connection pool, slow queries, cache hit rate — then fix the usual causes in order: N+1 queries, missing index, unbounded results, or a timeout-less downstream call.
tips: Lead with measurement, not with a fix.
Name the trap: scaling out before finding the bad query.
title: Scenario: suddenly slow API

detailedAnswer: The Java Memory Model defines happens-before relationships that guarantee when one thread's writes become visible to another: unlocking a monitor happens before a later lock of the same monitor, writing a volatile variable happens before a later read of it, and starting a thread happens before anything in that thread. Double-checked locking was broken before Java 5 because the instance reference could become visible before the constructor finished, letting another thread observe a partially constructed object. Declaring the field volatile fixes it, because the volatile write of the reference happens after construction and is visible only after the object is fully initialized. In practice, prefer an enum singleton, a static holder class, or dependency injection over hand-rolled double-checked locking, and never rely on timing or sleep to order visibility.
followUps: Why was double-checked locking broken before Java 5?
What is a safe alternative to double-checked locking?
question: Why did double-checked locking need volatile, and what does happens-before guarantee?
shortAnswer: Happens-before guarantees visibility between ordered actions; without volatile, another thread could see a partially constructed singleton, so volatile orders the reference publication after construction.
tips: Explain the partially constructed object problem concretely.
Recommend the enum singleton or static holder as the practical alternative.
title: Java Memory Model and double-checked locking
